what_its_for: Lactulose is a laxative used to treat constipation (difficulty having bowel movements). It is also used in people with liver disease to reduce the amount of ammonia in the blood, which can help prevent or treat a condition called hepatic encephalopathy (confusion or mental changes caused by liver problems).
how_to_take: Lactulose comes as a liquid syrup or as crystals you dissolve in water. Measure the liquid carefully using a proper measuring spoon or cup — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. You can mix the liquid or dissolved crystals with water, juice, or milk to improve the taste. Drink a full glass of water after each dose. Take it at the same time(s) each day to help you remember. You can take it with or without food.
dosing: For constipation, the usual adult dose is 15 to 30 mL (1 to 2 tablespoons) of liquid, or 10 to 20 grams of crystals, once daily. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how well it works for you — the goal is usually 1 to 3 soft bowel movements per day. For liver disease (hepatic encephalopathy), the dose is higher and is determined by your doctor. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly, and do not change your dose without talking to them first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at once to make up for the one you missed.
storage: Store lactulose liquid at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat and direct sunlight. Do not freeze the liquid — if it accidentally freezes, you can still use it after it thaws. The liquid may turn a slightly yellow or darker color over time, but this is normal and does not mean it has gone bad. Keep the bottle tightly closed and out of reach of children. Store crystal packets at room temperature in a dry place.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking other laxatives at the same time unless your doctor tells you to. Do not take antacids that contain aluminum (such as Maalox or Mylanta) at the same time as lactulose, as they may make it less effective. Avoid drinking alcohol while taking lactulose, especially if you have liver disease. Do not eat a very high sugar diet, as lactulose already contains sugars that can affect blood sugar levels — this is especially important if you have diabetes.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor if you experience severe stomach pain, cramping, or bloating that does not go away. Also call if you have diarrhea that is severe or lasts more than 2 days, if you have no bowel movement after 2 days of taking lactulose for constipation, if you notice blood in your stool, if you feel very weak or dizzy, or if you experience unusual thirst or decreased urination (signs of dehydration). If you have liver disease and notice increased confusion, call your doctor right away.
when_it_works: For constipation, lactulose usually produces a bowel movement within 24 to 48 hours after your first dose. It is not a fast-acting laxative, so be patient. For liver disease (hepatic encephalopathy), it may take 24 to 48 hours to see improvement in mental clarity. If you do not see results within 2 days for constipation, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to the effects of lactulose, especially dehydration and electrolyte imbalances — drink plenty of fluids. People with diabetes should be aware that lactulose contains small amounts of sugar (galactose and lactose), which may slightly affect blood sugar levels; monitor your blood sugar as directed. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before using lactulose, though it is generally considered safe. People with a condition called galactosemia (a rare sugar metabolism disorder) should NOT use lactulose. If you need a low-galactose diet, talk to your doctor before using this medication.
